# Incendiary weapons and Greek fire (`incendiaries_greek_fire`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by distillation, petroleum_refining, piston_pump
- Core idea: Byzantine Greek fire was a naval incendiary associated with the defence of Constantinople. Chroniclers describe burning liquid projected from ships and its frightening effect on crews. Earlier armies had used burning projectiles and vessels, and later Islamic and Chinese sources describe distinct incendiary traditions. The Byzantine fleet's advantage depended on trained crews, specialised ships and state supply. Petroleum is a plausible component, but the composition and equipment cannot be recovered with certainty from the texts.
- Pitfalls:
  - Water spreads burning oil; sand, earth, vinegar-soaked hides and felt were the historical defences
  - Greek fire was not gunpowder and contained no saltpetre as far as the evidence shows
  - The popular idea that it ignited on contact with water (quicklime) is not supported by the Byzantine sources
  - A heated, pressurised vessel of petroleum on a wooden ship is as dangerous to the user as to the enemy
  - Treating a modern experimental reconstruction as a measurement of the historical weapon
- History: mesopotamia: 9th c. BC – Assyrian reliefs show fire arrows and torches against siege engines; greece: 424 BC – Boeotians use a bellows-driven flame tube against the wooden wall at Delium (Thucydides IV.100); c. 672–678 – Greek fire, credited to Kallinikos of Heliopolis, saves Constantinople; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra lists incendiary mixtures and fire arrows; china: 919 – petrol flame-thrower (fierce fire oil) recorded; 1044 – Wujing Zongyao describes its double-acting piston pump; islamic: 8th–9th c. – corps of naphtha throwers (naffatun) in Abbasid armies; 12th c. – naphtha grenades against the Crusaders
- Read:
  - J. R. Partington, A History of Greek Fire and Gunpowder (1960)
  - John Haldon, 'Greek Fire' Revisited: Recent and Current Research, in E. Jeffreys (ed.), Byzantine Style, Religion and Civilization (2006)
  - Adrienne Mayor, Greek Fire, Poison Arrows & Scorpion Bombs (2003)
